newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Taleban face new kind of guerrilla war.
newsitem.headline: Taleban face new kind of guerrilla war.

text.p: Afghanistan's Taleban militia faced forces using its own guerrilla tactics as fighters loyal to former military chief Ahmad Shah Masood attacked supply lines north of the city, witnesses said on Saturday.

Local commanders spurred on by Masood cut a vital highway running from Kabul to the Taleban's northern frontline against the forces of Masood and militia chief Abdul Rashid Dostum on Friday, employing hit-and-run tactics the Taleban have not previously faced.

"Taleban hold some parts of the road between here and Kabul and we hold some," Masood commander Abdul Bashir Salanghi said in Olang, just south of the Salang Pass which marks the entrance to Dostum's stronghold.

Dostum has yet to commit his well-equipped forces to the conflict but signed an agreement on Thursday with Masood and another local militia commander, Karim Khalili, pledging to support each other if attacked.

The Taleban, a purist Islamic militia that swept from the south to take Kabul a fortnight ago after overrunning much of the country, have found their supply lines under attack from local commanders and fighters apparently coordinated by Masood.

Masood emerged earlier this week from his native Panjsher Valley some 80 km (50 miles) north of Kabul, where he had been holed up since the Taleban takeover, to strike at Taleban positions north of Jabal-os-Siraj in fierce fighting.
Local residents and Taleban fighters said he had also persuaded local commanders not disarmed by the Taleban to strike at towns, positions, convoys and a military base along the highway.
It was not immediately clear on Saturday whether they had held their positions, advanced or retreated to hills and villages some distance from the road.

Salanghi said on Friday his forces may launch assaults on Jabal-os-Siraj, a key town at a fork in the road leading to Salang in the north, the Panjsher in the east, and Kabul to the south, and Charikar, a town halfway along the Kabul highway.

The Taleban, applauded by some Afghans for the security they brought to areas under their control, said on Friday they had imposed a 9 p.m. to 5 a.m. curfew on the capital, particularly for "journalists who make wrong reports".

The Taleban have reacted harshly to what they say is a hostile campaign by western media and governments against its movement, a campaign they say is driven by misunderstandings of its Islamic rules and journalists' abuse of their hospitality.

Western governments have been cautious in their response to Taleban rule. Some have expressed concern over harsh restrictions on the role of women, saying it would jeopardise aid for the war-ravaged country.
France called on Friday for an end to civil strife in Afghanistan and the creation of a coalition government.

The United Nations General Assembly deferred a decision on the credentials of Afghanistan's U.N. delegation, leaving in place for the moment the representatives of ousted President Burhanuddin Rabbani, Masood's political mentor.
The Taleban's strident rhetoric appears to have softened in recent days, with Taleban leaders offering cautious support to a U.N. ceasefire and talks.
In their Thursday meeting Dostum, Masood and Khalili also called for setting up of a "permanent government" and agreed to establish a Supreme Defence Council, leaving its composition to a later date.
The Taleban have been anxious to avoid provoking Dostum, a former communist military chief, who has yet to commit his forces defending the Salang pass to battle.
Until recent reverses they appeared set on dislodging Masood from his stronghold but have been thrown onto the defensive by attacks behind their lines.

Taleban fighters, fired by religious fervour and used to sweeping advances, have found themselves harried by small well-armed units using the guerrilla tactics perfected by Masood in his successful attacks on Soviet forces in the 1980s.
Afghan watchers said the fate of the Taleban, the latest in a line of Afghan governments under siege, now depended on how fast they could adapt their tactics to the new situation.
